name: Chemical Systems
tagline: Complex reaction networks, oscillators, and far-from-equilibrium chemistry.
seo_title: Chemical Systems — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Chemical Systems on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in reaction networks, oscillating reactions, patterns and far-from-equilibrium chemistry.

definition.lead: Chemical Systems explores reactions that do not simply go from A to B: networks with feedback, oscillating clocks, travelling waves, patterns and chaos.
definition.body: Far from equilibrium, chemistry can keep time, form stripes and spots, and even compute. The same principles help explain heartbeats, circadian rhythms and the patterns on animal coats.

timeline.title: Oscillations in theory
timeline.text: Alfred Lotka shows a simple reaction scheme can oscillate indefinitely.

timeline.title: An early oscillating reaction
timeline.text: William Bray reports oscillations in the reaction of hydrogen peroxide and iodate.

timeline.title: Belousov's reaction
timeline.text: Boris Belousov observes a solution that oscillates in colour; his paper is rejected.
timeline.why: Later developed by Anatol Zhabotinsky into the BZ reaction.

timeline.title: Turing's morphogenesis
timeline.text: Alan Turing shows that reaction and diffusion can create patterns.
timeline.why: A chemical theory of biological pattern.

timeline.title: The Brusselator
timeline.text: Ilya Prigogine and René Lefever propose a model oscillating reaction.
timeline.why: A simple model of chemical oscillations.

timeline.title: The BZ mechanism
timeline.text: Richard Field, Endre Kőrös and Richard Noyes explain the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction.

timeline.title: Briggs–Rauscher
timeline.text: A vivid colour-oscillating reaction is introduced for classrooms.

timeline.title: Nobel Prize
timeline.text: Ilya Prigogine is honoured for non-equilibrium thermodynamics.

timeline.title: Turing patterns in a gel
timeline.text: Patrick De Kepper's group observes stationary Turing patterns experimentally.

quiz.q: What does the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction do?
options: Its colour oscillates periodically
It explodes after a short delay
It glows green in the dark
It freezes and melts in cycles
quiz.explain: It can also form spiral waves in a thin layer.

options: Reactions combined with diffusion at different rates
Gravity pulling heavier molecules into stripes
Magnetic fields aligning the reacting molecules
Random noise alone, with no chemistry involved
quiz.explain: A slow activator and a fast inhibitor.

quiz.q: What does a chemical oscillation need?
options: Conditions far from equilibrium, and feedback
Conditions exactly at chemical equilibrium
Freezing temperatures to slow the reaction down
A single reaction with no feedback at all
quiz.explain: Near equilibrium, reactions simply settle down.

quiz.q: Why can't a closed system oscillate forever?
options: It inevitably approaches equilibrium
It runs out of space
The colours fade
It explodes
quiz.explain: Sustained oscillations need a continuous supply of reactants.

No feedback

quiz.q: Why use a continuous stirred-tank reactor to study oscillations?
options: It supplies reactants continuously, keeping the system far from equilibrium
It is cheaper than any other type of reactor
It removes coloured products as soon as they form
It cools the reaction to stop it overheating

quiz.q: When were stationary Turing patterns first seen experimentally?
quiz.explain: In the CIMA reaction in a gel.

quiz.q: Spiral waves in a BZ dish resemble…
options: Waves of electrical activity in heart tissue during some arrhythmias
Ocean waves driven by wind over long distances
Sound waves travelling through a solid material
Radio waves emitted by the reacting molecules
quiz.explain: The same mathematics of excitable media.
